method: Rebuild from primary text. 26 C.F.R. §1.83-2 was fetched from the eCFR, which is the Office of the Federal Register's official electronic Code of Federal Regulations, and read in full. 26 U.S.C. §83 was fetched from uscode.house.gov, the Office of the Law Revision Counsel. IRS Form 15620 (Rev. 4-2025) was downloaded from irs.gov and its text extracted; the extraction was partial and is flagged below. Assertions describe the REBUILT body.
queries: "83(b) election" property transferred in connection with performance of services gross income

assertions.text: the election is filed with the internal revenue office with which the person performing the services files their return
assertions.note: Treas. Reg. §1.83-2(c), verbatim: 'The election referred to in paragraph (a) of this section is made by filing one copy of a written statement with the internal revenue office with which the person who performed the services files his return.' Form 15620's instructions say the same. The previous body said the election must be 'postmarked to the IRS office' — see priorDefects.

assertions.text: the deadline is not later than 30 days after the date the property was transferred, and the election may be filed before the transfer
assertions.note: Treas. Reg. §1.83-2(b), and 26 U.S.C. §83(b)(2): 'An election under paragraph (1) with respect to any transfer of property shall be made in such manner as the Secretary prescribes and shall be made not later than 30 days after the date of such transfer.' The previous body did not mention that early filing is permitted.

assertions.text: the 30 days is fixed by the statute, so the regulations provide no extension and no cure
assertions.note: §83(b)(2) sets the period, and nothing in §1.83-2 provides for an extension. Stated on that narrower ground rather than on the broader claim about discretionary relief — see gaps.

assertions.text: the statement must be signed, must say it is made under section 83(b), and must contain seven specified items
assertions.note: Treas. Reg. §1.83-2(e)(1)-(7): name, address and TIN; a description of each property; the date or dates of transfer and the taxable year; the nature of the restrictions; the fair market value at transfer determined without regard to any lapse restriction; the amount paid; and, for elections after July 21, 1978, a statement that copies have been furnished as required by §1.83-2(d). The previous body — a clause titled 'Filing Instructions' inside an 83(b) election document — contained none of them.

assertions.text: a copy must be submitted to the person for whom the services are performed, and to the transferee of the property where that is a different person
assertions.note: Treas. Reg. §1.83-2(d). The previous body said 'Provide a copy to the Company for its records', which presents a regulatory requirement as a courtesy — and §1.83-2(e)(7) makes a statement that the copies were furnished part of the election's required content, so failing to do it is not a filing-hygiene issue.

assertions.text: the election may not be revoked except with the Commissioner's consent, given only for a mistake of fact as to the underlying transaction and only if requested within 60 days of the date the mistake first became known
assertions.note: Treas. Reg. §1.83-2(f), verbatim, including that a mistake as to value, a decline in value, or a failure to perform an act contemplated at the time of transfer is not a mistake of fact. 26 U.S.C. §83(b)(2) also says the election 'may not be revoked except with the consent of the Secretary'. Absent from the previous body.

assertions.text: the IRS publishes Form 15620, which may be used instead of a written statement
assertions.note: Form 15620 (Rev. 4-2025), 'Section 83(b) Election', Catalog Number 95376D, downloaded from irs.gov. Its instructions read in part 'Submit this completed and signed Form 15620 to the IRS via mail with the IRS office with which the person who performs the services files a federal income tax return' and, under Who May File, offer the form as an alternative ('In the alternative, an 83(b) ...'). This was the clause's recorded defect and it is now in the body.

assertions.text: paying full fair market value does not preclude the election, and the election is what keeps later appreciation out of ordinary income
assertions.note: Treas. Reg. §1.83-2(a): 'The fact that the transferee has paid full value for the property transferred, realizing no bargain element in the transaction, does not preclude the use of the election as provided for in this section.' Alves v. Commissioner quotes that sentence and holds §83 applies to a taxpayer who bought restricted stock at full value as an investment: 'A taxpayer wishing to avoid treatment of appreciation as ordinary income must make an affirmative election under 83(b) in the year the stock was acquired.' This is why the clause exists — founder stock is usually bought at or near fair market value, and without Alves a reader could think there is nothing to elect about.

assertions.text: if the property is later forfeited no deduction is allowed, and the loss is limited to the excess of what was paid over what was realised
assertions.note: 26 U.S.C. §83(b)(1) flush language, applied in Kadillak v. Commissioner: 'the flush language of § 83(b)(1) expressly disallows any deduction respecting the forfeiture of his non-vested shares that were subject to his valid § 83(b) election.' Treas. Reg. §1.83-2(a) supplies the loss measure. This is the downside of the election and no version of this clause has stated it.

priorDefects: imprecise: 'must be postmarked to the IRS office ... within thirty (30) days'. §1.83-2(b) and §83(b)(2) speak of the election being MADE or FILED within 30 days, and §1.83-2(c) of filing a copy with the office. Whether a postmark is a filing is governed by 26 U.S.C. §7502, which was NOT read.
understated: 'Provide a copy to the Company for its records.' §1.83-2(d) requires it, and §1.83-2(e)(7) makes a statement that copies were furnished a required content element of the election itself.
omitted: all seven required content items in §1.83-2(e).
omitted: that the election may be filed before the transfer (§1.83-2(b)).
omitted: the revocation rule and its 60-day window (§1.83-2(f)).
omitted: Form 15620 — already recorded as a defect and not repaired.
omitted: that a copy also goes to the transferee where the service provider and the transferee differ.

omitted: that a forfeiture after a valid election yields no deduction (§83(b)(1)) and a loss limited to the excess of the amount paid over the amount realised (§1.83-2(a)). The clause instructs a founder to file and never says what filing costs if the stock is forfeited.
gaps: 26 U.S.C. §7502, the timely-mailing-is-timely-filing rule, was not read. The rebuilt body therefore tells the reader to send the election in a way that produces a dated record, and does not assert that a postmark is a filing.

Treas. Reg. §301.9100 was not read. The clause's claim that there is no cure for a late filing is stated on the narrower and verified ground that the 30-day period comes from the statute; whether §301.9100 relief is unavailable for that reason was not verified.

Form 15620's instruction text extracted only partially from the PDF — the 'Who May File' and 'When to File' paragraphs came through as fragments. What is asserted about the form is limited to the fragments that did extract cleanly. irs.gov is the agency and not a publisher of law.
State law was not considered. A California taxpayer may have a separate state filing obligation and nothing here addresses it.

The remaining substantive consequences in §1.83-2(a) — that the substantial vesting rules of §83(a) stop applying, and the basis rule for a later sale — were read and are not carried. Whether another clause in the election document states them was not checked.

judicialQuotations.quote: Moreover, nothing in section 83(b) precludes a taxpayer who has paid full market value for restricted stock from making an 83(b) election.

The tax laws often make an affirmative election necessary. Section 83(b) is but one example of a provision requiring taxpayers to act or suffer less attractive tax consequences. A taxpayer wishing to avoid treatment of appreciation as ordinary income must make an affirmative election under 83(b) in the year the stock was acquired.

the flush language of § 83(b)(1) expressly disallows any deduction respecting the forfeiture of his non-vested shares that were subject to his valid § 83(b) election. The statute plainly states: "If such election is made, ... and if such property is subsequently forfeited, no deduction shall be allowed in respect of such forfeiture."

caseLawNote: CourtListener was searched twice. A search on the regulation and the 30-day deadline returned nothing — no decision construing the mechanics of filing was found, which is consistent with §1.83-2 being procedural. A second search on the election itself returned a body of federal law, of which two decisions bear on this clause: Alves, on whether an election is available where full value was paid, and Kadillak, on what a later forfeiture costs. Neither construes the filing rules the clause states; both supply consequences the clause was silent about, and both are now in it.
